newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: E.Asian Grain - S.Korea seeking more Chinese corn.
newsitem.headline: E.Asian Grain - S.Korea seeking more Chinese corn.

text.p: South Korean buyers plan to pick up more Chinese corn for August/September shipment while interest in U.S.-origin has dried up due to high Chicago futures prices, traders said on Monday.
"We are in negotiations with suppliers to buy more Chinese corn," a trader with a major South Korean feed mill firm said.
South Korean buyers have bought an estimated 885,500 tonnes of Chinese corn through tenders and private negotiations since January, the dealers said.
Chinese corn is more attractive than U.S. grain because of its lower price and the fact that shipment times are faster with Chinese ports just a few days sailing from South Korea.
Smaller vessels can also be used to ship corn from China to minor South Korean ports, which make it easier for local feed milling companies to manage their grain inventories.
Dry bulk freight rates from the U.S. Pacific Northwest to South Korea were quoted unchanged at around US$14.50 a tonne. Rates from the U.S. Gulf also remained flat at $24.50 a tonne.
Japanese buyers were also watching the price gap between Chinese and U.S. corn. Japan has almost finished covering its April/June requirements of U.S. corn, Tokyo traders said.
U.S. corn premiums for Japan were quoted at about 97 U.S. cents a bushel over the CBOT May contract.
Wheat and canola traders in Tokyo said grain shipments from Canada's west coast are gradually returning to normal.
Heavy snow, extreme cold, and equipment failure have led to delays in rail shipments to Pacific ports from grain-growing regions in Canada since early January.
Japan's Food Agency chief said last Friday it would not cut imports from Canada as a result.
"We're still confident of Canada's stable grain supply capacity," Yuki Takagi, the agency's top official, said.
"Some wheat flour makers in Japan were worried about possible supply shortages, but the worst is now behind us," a wheat trader in Tokyo said.
In Taiwan, traders said they expect to see one tender this week for a combined shipment of 30,000 tonnes of soybeans and corn by the Taiwan Sugar Corp. The delivery date is May 1-15.
The Taiwan Flour Mills Association, however, is expected to remain sidelined this week, traders said.
In the Philippines, grain importers are expected to stay away from the market and shift to other sources of wheat and soybeans if prices in the United States remain high this week, dealers said.
"We are actually reviewing the offer for Canadian wheat and South American soybean due to high prices in the United State," an official at a local flour mill said.
